ABSTRACT
Due to the recent advancements in high-­speed networks, underlying hardware computing resources and resource scheduling 
algorithms, Cloud computing has emerged as a popular computing paradigm globally providing end-­user services such as in-
frastructure, hardware platforms and application tools. Subsequently, the researchers across various domains have integrated 
different services to facilitate the end users. However, the real issue faced by the cloud infrastructure is the network latency due 
to the physical dispersion between clients and cloud data centers. According to an estimate, billions of internet of things (IoT) 
devices are sharing approximately two exabytes of data daily. Such a huge amount of data can affect network performance if 
the underlying physical system does not expand up to the required levels, leading to performance degradation. To overcome 
these issues, a new computing paradigm called Fog Computing has emerged in recent years. In this paper, we discuss the recent 
developments in fog computing with the integration of real-­time Healthcare 5.0 technology. Furthermore, we describe the pro-
posed layered architecture and taxonomy of resource management (RM) techniques in fog computing, which consists of energy 
awareness, scheduling, reliability and scalability. Besides that, our survey covers the three-­tier layered architecture, evaluation 
metrics, real-­time application aspects of fog computing and tools providing the implementation of RM techniques in fog com-
puting. Furthermore, the proposed layered architecture of the standard fog framework and different state-­of-­the-­art techniques 
for utilising the computing resources of fog networks have been covered in this study. Moreover, we include various sensors to 
demonstrate the fog data offloading example in healthcare 5.0 applications. We also present a thorough discussion on various 
current and future real-­time applications of fog computing. Finally, open challenges and promising future research directions 
have been identified and discussed in the area of fog-­based real-­time applications.

1   |   Introduction
Modern-­day computing paradigms like cloud, fog and edge have 
enormous advantages for real-­time applications. Real-­time appli-
cations like smart transportation, smart farming and health care 
need quick responses for effective and efficient execution of end-­
user tasks. Healthcare applications are most sensitive and require 
rapid response time for healthcare patients. The transition and 
rapid increase in computational abilities of systems have urged 
individuals and organisations to rely on computers for automa-
tion and computations (Naha et al. 2018). With the advent of the 
new computing paradigm called the internet of things (IoT), nu-
merous devices connected to the Internet, such as sensors and 
actuators, are producing enormous data on daily a basis. These 
electronic devices are an integral part of IoT, working in an envi-
ronment to collect data, communicate with each other, and then 
send it to the cloud sources for further processing and decisions 
(Rauf et  al.  2018). Billions of IoT devices are generating data 
into the cloud for processing, and they require faster responses 
equally. The cloud is the utility computing providing services to 
the users in the form of software as a service (SaaS), platform 
as a service (PaaS) and infrastructure as a service (IaaS). The 
main component of cloud computing is its data centres (DCs) 
that store huge amounts of data requested by its users globally. 
Millions of companies, organisations and individuals are sending 
real-­time data to cloud DCs for analytics and decision-­making. 
The process of data storage, processing and sending it back to the 
clients requires time which is considered as a delay. This delay 
or latency sensitivity is a major drawback that the cloud is still 
facing. To overcome this issue, the researchers are finding new 
approaches to computing paradigms, namely cloudlets, fog com-
puting, edge computing, or mobile edge computing. These par-
adigms have many characteristics that distinguish them from 
cloud computing. All these paradigms lie under the concept of 
cloud computing (Mouradian et al. 2017). Fog computing is a de-
centralised computing paradigm where all the processing is done 
at the edges of devices, also termed IoT devices. These IoT de-
vices include smartphones, routers, switches and others that can 
process, storage capacity, or even a fog device. Table 1 includes 
the acronyms and their abbreviations used in this survey paper.
Several surveys related to fog-­computing taxonomy, ar-
chitecture and various application areas have been pre-
sented. However, none of the studies investigated the 
multi-­dimensional aspects of fog computing in a single article. 
This paper motivates the author and provides a complete pack-
age in the fog-­computing paradigm, including fog-­computing 
architecture, the taxonomy of fog-­computing layering archi-
tecture, healthcare 5.0 technology, other real-­time applica-
tions domains, the taxonomy of fault tolerance and simulation 
tools in fog computing. Furthermore, it also provides a thor-
ough review of the recent developments in the fog-­computing 
paradigm, including the layered architecture and resource 
management (RM) techniques. Furthermore, it explores the 
fog systems from the perspective of energy awareness, task 
scheduling, load balancing, reliability and scalability. In addi-
tion to that, numerous application domains like smart cities, 
smart transportation systems, smart healthcare, smart farm-
ing, and augmented and virtual reality play a vital role in fog-­
computing architecture.

2   |   Fog Computing
Fog computing is the extended version of cloud computing and 
is a decentralised computing concept where computation is per-
formed at the edges of IoT devices. These devices can perform 
computation and storage capacity like cloud computing DCs. Fog 
computing is the emergent computing concept in recent research 
studies which unlike cloud computing does not rely on any cen-
tral component (Naha et al. 2018). Fog-­computing concept was 
introduced by cisco in 2012 in order to come up with a challenge 
that billions of geographically distributed IoT devices require 
high computation power and storage capacity for real-­time ap-
plications. Although fog computing and cloud computing have 
similarities in terms of services provided by both paradigms, the 
fog has one major distinguishing characteristic than cloud that it 
is very close to the end-­users. Data generated by end devices sent 
to fog computing for computation and storage, however, utilisa-
tion of resources at the edges will not replace cloud computing 
(Kumar et al. 2019). As both are the reinforcement of each other. 
Fog also uses the concept of virtualisation. A virtualised platform 
that is tightly linked or located to the cloud and end-­users and 
does not work in a standalone mode unlike other computing par-
adigms like cloudlets and multi-­access edge computing (MEC). It 
also provides reduced latency, Quality of service (QoS), and en-
ergy consumption over the internet (Saharan and Kumar 2015).

3   |   Healthcare 5.0: A Prospective Transmission
The revolution in various domain like smart cities, transportation, 
industry 4.0, and healthcare system becomes possible by adopting 
smart technologies. The paradigm shift in healthcare system from 
generation to generation witnessed the transition from healthcare 
1.0 to healthcare 5.0. In healthcare 1.0, medical records were based 
on doctor-­centric and manually generated. Healthcare 2.0 system 
converted from doctor-­centric to patients-­centric, where all man-
ually medical records were managed electronically also known 
as electronic health records (EHRs). The EHRs were stored in a 
decentralised manner and managed through mobile applications 
in healthcare 3.0. However, healthcare 3.0 lacked real-­time ana-
lytics and subject to malicious attacks. Healthcare 4.0 integrate AI 
with big data for effective analysis and decision making on stored 
EHRs. However, the integration of AI with big data becomes com-
plicated and less responsive with the increase of medical data. 
Healthcare 5.0 provide a patients-­centric, ultra responsive solution 
with the integration of IoT, 5G/6G communications and secure 
business model. Figure 1 shows the healthcare transition history 
from 1.0 to 5.0.
The primary concern of the healthcare 5.0 is a patient-­centric 
and keep them in healthcare system. All the medical suppliers 
are made possible due to physicians, clinics, patients and med-
ical warehouses. Healthcare 5.0 technology made possible the 
cost-­effective delivery of healthcare services to end-­user con-
sumers with no delay. Many different sensors are integrated 
with healthcare 5.0 technology to support virtual healthcare sys-
tem. These diverse sensors have the capability to improve and 
speed up healthcare service deliveries.

4.1   |   Proposed Architecture of Cloud-­Fog-­IoT
Figure 2 shows the proposed architecture of n-­tier computing.
The top-­tier is the cloud layer which consists of large DCs for 
massive operations and long-­term storage purposes. Most real-­
time operations send their data for quick response. However, 
due to long distance geographic location and multi-­hop distance, 
the cloud produces communication latency for real-­time appli-
cations which is unacceptable to end-­users. The second layer, i.e. 
fog layer, is an important layer of the architecture, where all the 
devices are responsible for computation, storage and communi-
cate over the network. The devices responsible for processing 
and short-­term storage purposes can be routers, switches, PC's, 
modems, workstations and servers, etc. Virtualisation concept 
can be used in this layer like cloud computing. The third tier is 
the IoT layer where billions of smart devices and gadgets gener-
ate data and send to Fog layer for real-­time processing. The fog 
computing with the integration of IoT devices brings benefits to 
time-­sensitive IoT applications and hence reduce latency (Atlam 
et al. 2018). Many IoT infrastructures like energy management, 
product tracking, e-­healthcare, smart grids, smart vehicular sys-
tem and others demand real-­time processing and low latency 
services from providers, as compared to the traditional cloud 
computing which relies on DCs for computation and storage. 
The spontaneous reaction from DCs to IoT application is diffi-
cult due to the massive amount of data generated by IoT devices, 
creating a bottleneck and poor QoS. So traditional cloud com-
puting is not a viable solution to overcome this issue after the 
growing demands of IoT devices (Sarkar et al. 2015). According 
to an estimate, 50 billion IoT devices will connect to the inter-
net in 2020 (Ni et al. 2017) and it will increase up to 500 billion 
end devices by 2025 (Camhi 2015). The voluminous increase in 
end devices in recent times does not impact the users’ request. 
Fog layer takes responsibility for what data send to the cloud 
and what is not. However, cloud is responsible for doing complex 
processing.

5   |   RM in fog Computing
RM is one of the key aspects of providing efficient resources 
to physical hardware and important phenomena in any com-
puting paradigm. Various research articles are published 
on RM in cloud computing. Fog computing is the extension 
of cloud computing and like cloud, the resources are shared 
and virtualised in fog computing as well. Some of the met-
rics/techniques considered for main research challenges are 
energy-­aware, resource allocation, load balancing, network-­
aware, mobile fog computing, and so forth (Naha et al. 2018; 
Mouradian et al. 2017).
The main focus of this section is to present the following RM 
metrics in detail and highlight major contributions of these met-
rics in the world of Fog computing.

5.1   |   Energy-­Aware RM in Fog Computing
Energy efficiency is one of the main concerns so far, that com-
puting paradigms faced a lot and is increasing demand to be 
considered for research perspective (Fiandrino et  al.  2015). 
Communication technologies and information systems increas-
ing day-­by-­day and there is immense need to reduce the energy 
consumption of storage and computation by applying energy-­
efficient techniques (Berl et  al.  2010). We will discuss some 
energy-­aware RM techniques in Fog computing in the succeed-
ing section.
Oma et al. (2018) proposed a linear model to a sequence of Fog 
nodes and Fog server. The linear IoT model used for the evalua-
tion of total execution time and total electric energy consumption 
of the nodes as compared with the cloud computing system. 
The evaluation result shows that the proposed model reduced 
the total electric energy consumption as compared to the cloud 
model. Tactile internet is an emerging concept between human-­
to-­machine interactions due to its responsive, high allegiance 
and availability nature. Fog computing is an integral part of 
the tactile internet due to its low transmission latency. Xiao 
and Krunz  (2018) present the efficient energy design of Fog-­
computing network that support tactile internet applications 
due to low transmission latency. Two performance metrics ser-
vice response time and power usage efficiency were investigated 
with a trade-­off amongst two metrics. A novel concept referred 
to as workload offloading was introduced in which different en-
ergy resources and Fog nodes cooperate with each other. The 
purpose of this cooperation is to balance the workload amongst 
Fog nodes thereby reducing service response time and power 
usage efficiency. Two distributed optimisation algorithms were 
introduced to achieve optimum trade-­off between two metrics. 
One algorithm is based on the sub-­gradient method having 
dual decomposition and other is based on alternating direction 
method multiplied through variable splitting (ADMM-­VS). Both 
the algorithms proved that optimum workload offloading can be 
achieved by reducing response time and power usage efficiency.
Fog-­computing architecture enables IoT applications and 5G 
communication with an enormous number of mobile devices 
exchanging frequent communication handovers to one another 
thus resulting in considerable load on the underlying network 
entities. Existing distributed mobility management (DMM) 
solutions provide smooth handovers but lack in security issues. 
Sharma et  al.  (2018) proposed a new DMM schema based on 
Blockchain. The new DMM schema can resolve security issues 
less affecting the network layout and also assuring the energy-­
efficient distributed security requirements. This Blockchain 
DMM has a significant impact on reducing real-­time signalling 
burden as compared to DMM solutions.

5.2   |   Resource Allocation in Fog Computing
Resource allocation and scheduling are important for efficient 
utilisation of resources and managing load balancing in DSs (Xu 
et al. 2018, 2020). Resource allocation in fog computing means 
to optimise the utilisation of resources in fog-­computing nodes. 
Resource allocation and scheduling techniques for fog-­computing 
nodes enable each other to cooperate for better resource utilisa-
tion (Zhang and Li 2018). The absolute aim of resource allocation 
is to optimise the number of resources and balancing the work-
load amongst active physical machines (Li and Zhang 2016).
Carbon footprint is the emission of carbon dioxide into the at-
mosphere due to geographically distributed DCs for real-­time 
applications. The immense amount of carbon footprint is a chal-
lenge to all researchers to protecting the atmosphere further. 
Cloud computing DCs omit massive carbon footprints and are 
dangerous to the world. The huge amount of data traffic from 
billions of devices put pressure on DCs for immediate response. 
Various researchers give numerous techniques and approaches 
to overcome this issue, however, the issue is getting worst due 
to increase in devices. To overcome this issue, DCs must be geo-
graphically distributed and task should be allocated uniformly 
not to decrease the traffic but also reduce carbon footprint. Do 
et  al.  (2015) developed a distributed algorithm and ADMM. 
These two algorithms are developed to solve a large-­scale prob-
lem of resource allocation and reducing carbon footprint for 
real-­time video-­streaming applications in geographically dis-
tributed Fog computing. The algorithm performance was evalu-
ated through numerical results.
QoS is the growing demand for modern high-­performance com-
puting (HPC), to ensure a better quality of service for end-­users 
and allocating efficient resources to different IoT applications. 
Abedin et al. (2018) proposed a new analytic hierarchy process 
(AHP) based on matching games. Using AHP, matching games 
are used to stable association between Fog devices and IoT de-
vices. The best-­fit resource allocation strategy was applied to 
solve network resource allocation issue during the matching 
process. The simulated results show that the performance of 
best-­fit resource allocation strategy gains significantly good QoS 
compared to other conventional strategies.
Zafar et al. (2018) proposed a new Fog cloud-­based model for 
efficient utilisation of resource allocation to clusters in close 
proximity to residential buildings in the world. The aim of work 
is the energy management for smart homes requirement and 
micro grids (MGs) used to balance the load on Fog and reduce 
wastage of resources further. The authors proposed a new bio-­
inspired bat algorithm (BA) method used to balance the load on 
Fog using virtual machines (VMs). The proposed algorithm was 
evaluated using cloud analyst simulator, and the results were 
compared with particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and active 
VM load balancer (AVLB) and analysed that proposed algorithm 
perform better than others.
Khan et al. (2022) proposed an optimal resource allocation and 
load-­balancing strategy for real-­time healthcare applications in 
fog-­computing environment. The proposed strategy optimises 
the end-­to-­end delay for healthcare application delay sensitive 
in order to reduce the energy consumption, network bandwidth 
utilisation. However, the system can adopt some evolutionary 
techniques for delay-­sensitive health applications to enhance 
overall system performance.
5.3   |   Scheduling in Fog Computing
Scheduling is an important characteristic of RM. Many dis-
tributed computing brings new challenges in scheduling and 
grabs the attention of researchers. Many different applications 
run in any computing environment require proper scheduling 
mechanism. Scheduling is the strategy which decides to share 
resources amongst various activities or tasks in the available 
pool of resources. Various scheduling strategies relating to Fog 
computing are discussed in this section.
Bitam et al. (2018) proposed a new bees life algorithm (BLA) 
approach to address job scheduling problem in fog computing. 
Job schedule acts as an operating and management functions 
providing high performance and cost-­effective services to end-­
users and fog computing nodes. The proposed approach dis-
tributes tasks amongst Fog nodes. The purpose of proposed 
approach is to find an optimal solution in terms of CPU exe-
cution time and allocated memory for fog-­computing nodes. 
The evaluation results show that the performance of proposed 
BLA approach demonstrates better compared to conventional 
algorithms.
Real-­time big data processing in an industrial environment 
is the main challenge nowadays. As the computation para-
digms transform from cloud to fog, it distributes computing 
resources over a wide geographic range. To address the non-­
negligible and limited computation power issue in Fog nodes, 
Wang et al. (2019) proposed a data scheduling approach based 
on optimisation. This policy is based on using multiple chan-
nels of communication to reduce real-­time latency and en-
hance system stability. Various tests designed to evaluate 
the performance of scheduling policies and results show that 
the performance of the proposed scheduling policy can gain 
significantly.
Razzaq et al. (2019) discussed various scheduling algorithms for 
high performance computing (HPC) to efficient utilise comput-
ing resources. The authors focused in the paper on two factors. 
First, the scheduling algorithms classification on the basis of 
several parameters like response time, CPU utilisation, through-
put, scalability and cost-­effectiveness, and these were investi-
gated from period 2009 to 2017. The purpose of categorisation is 
to provide a simple view of HPC. The second factor predicts the 
growth of HPC applications for 2020 and beyond.

5.4   |   Reliability in Fog Computing
Reliability is a major concern for modern distributed systems 
and is essential for customer satisfaction and confidence and in-
habiting loses (Mesbahi et al. 2018). It also handles the reliability 
measures and metrics of various systems. So, reliability is an im-
portant RM factor to handle the fog-­computing complex system 
(Naha et al. 2018).
Latency, location awareness and the ability to detect unexpected 
real-­time events are the serious issues that cloud is unable to 
solve. Fog computing enables the deployment of real-­time ap-
plications and services. Vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs) 
offering new computing trends and opportunities and thus 
fog computing is able to meet VANETs requirement. Pereira 
et al. (2019) proposed an architecture for fog-­computing services 
and applications deployed in VANETs environment. Besides 
that, the authors provide a proof-­of-­concept system for data anal-
ysis in VANET/Fog environment. The provided system used two 
fog applications. One is the anomaly detection in city traffic and 
other is time estimation information of bus arrival to travellers. 
The performance and reliability of the two applications are val-
idated through real deployment of 600 vehicles in Portugal. The 
evaluation results show that fog computing is suitable for these 
two applications and also provide reliable network performance 
in considerable period of time.
VANETs technology improves the number of traffic road acci-
dents and dissatisfaction amongst users. The purpose to intro-
duce VANETs technology is to exchange traffic information 
amongst vehicles through sensor networks. Information trans-
mission between terminal nodes and DC producing latency 
needs to be addressed. Chiang et al. (2018) proposed three-­layer 
fog-­ computing network architecture. The proposed architec-
ture aims to get traffic information with low latency for users.
5.5   |   Scalability in Fog Computing
Scalability is an important aspect of many computing para-
digms. Like in clouds, scalability changes the cloud applica-
tions in terms of volume, size and geographic distribution to 
meet customer needs (Campbell et al. 2018). Since cloud deals 
scalability horizontally while Fog computing deals both hor-
izontally and vertically. Fog computing has the scalability 
issue which arises due to the increase in number of IoT devices 
day by day. Therefore, to tackle the current issue, Fog needs 
to scale up the services and devices to capacitate maximum 
devices.
Akrivopoulos et al. (2018) presented an IoT-­based fog-­computing 
architecture and deployed and evaluated it in a real-­world en-
vironment using several IoT devices. The performance of the 
proposed architecture conducted in the initial phase of up to 18 
schools indicates that the number can increase up to five times 
more that can handle network traffic. The proposed architec-
ture ensures the scalability of deployment in Fog computing 
using IoT devices.
Coutinho et al. (2018) present a fog-­computing framework with 
the integration of toolset for enabling fog testbeds in distributed 
virtualised environment. The design of the proposed framework 
meets the requirement of real-­world environment with low-­cost 
flexible setup. The integration of framework and toolset enables 
the fog components to be deployed and tested in a scalable way.

techniques mainly consists of resource allocation, task schedul-
ing, load balancing, scalability and reliability are the top areas in

7   |   Other Applications of Fog Computing
Besides the applications of fog computing in the field of smart 
health care, it possesses other application areas that it has con-
tributed widely and still it has contributed immensely. In this 
section, we discuss some research works and address some of 
the typical applications of fog computing applied in diverse 
areas and how these application areas overcome the major lim-
itations of fog computing as shown in Table 7.
7.1   |   Smart Transportation
Fog computing plays a significance role in the field of smart 
transportation. We discuss a few research works that have 
been done in fog-­based smart transportation and identify key 
limitations addressed by fog computing. Hou et al. (2016) pro-
posed infrastructure for vehicular fog computing to support 
different performance metrics and improve the performance 
of computation, communication and connectivity. Salonikias 
et  al.  (2015) identify operational characteristics and access 
control issue for intelligent transport system using fog comput-
ing, as real-­time applications require services, and movement 
of these services affects security and access control issues. 
For this reason, the authors present an attribute-­based access 
control scheme for fog computing. Lin et al. (2018) developed 
a model to allocate available bandwidth for different services 
required by vehicular fog computing. Shojafar et  al.  (2016) 
proposed a joint adaptive scheduler for the input output traffic 
and resource consolidation and reconfiguration of virtualised 
vehicular fog computing to maximise the overall energy effi-
ciency of computation plus communication with low transmis-
sion rates.
7.2   |   Smart Cities
Fog computing plays an important role in smart cities. In smart 
cities, factors like real-­time response and location awareness 
(Perera et al. 2013; Perera 2014) are important for incorporat-
ing context information (Pinjari et al. 2018). Some of the case 
studies are presented with the characteristic and limitations 
removed by fog computing. Merlino et  al.  (2014) designed an 
OpenStack-­framework spanning for (IaaS) and (PaaS) to enables 
developers and users to manage IoT infrastructure for multi-
ple location-­aware, low-­latency peer-­to-­peer IoT applications 
where most of the logic runs on smart objects. Li et al. (2015) 
proposed fog-­computing platform, namely EHOPES to improve 
the efficiency in terms of data transmission delay for real-­time 
applications that have strict delay requirements and quality of 
user experience in smart living. Giordano et al. (2016) present 
Rainbow architecture for development of smart city applications 
and to also cope with complexity and require management and 
control, monitoring and actionable information from real-­time 
issues. Chen et al. (2016) proposed fog-­computing-­based smart 
urban surveillance solution for vehicle tracking and its informa-
tion in real-­time for information extraction and quick decision 
making which is computationally complex, expensive and time 
consuming.
7.3   |   Smart Farming
Fog computing has a significant importance in the area of 
smart farming and agriculture. Smart farming using the exist-
ing technology and the deployment of low-­cost sensors attract 
more farmers and achieve sustainable productivity and growth. 
Malik et al. (2020) proposed a toolkit for modelling and simula-
tion of fog-­computing-­based distributed context-­aware complete 
farming ecosystem. The author designed framework for modern 
farming to facilitate users and simulate complete customised 
farming scenarios. Zamora-­Izquierdo et  al.  (2019) developed 
a three-­tier platform in real greenhouse in south-­east of Spain 
to manage precision agriculture (PA) and its main functional 
units. The demand of PA is increasing day by day. However, 
their usage is very limited due to high cost and not adoption in 
semi-­arid conditions. Sinha et al. (2023) presents a comprehen-
sive and thorough investigation of using fog-­computing meth-
odologies in smart agriculture systems and also proposed the 
challenges in networking, privacy and security issues. Similarly, 
Kethineni and Pradeepini  (2024) proposed a deep-­learning-­
based model to find DDoS attacks in smart farming systems. 
The proposed framework enhances the performance of farming 
system achieving better accuracy, precision and detection rate 
results.
7.4   |   Extended Reality (XR)
Fog computing plays a vital role for time-­sensitive applications. 
In this regard, the XR (augmented, virtual and mixed reality ap-
plications are extremely time-­sensitive) cannot afford delay and 
stalling (freezing of frames) (Anwar et al. 2019, 2020). The high-­
quality XR content and their application in smart transportation 
(Anwar, Choi, et al. 2024), education (Anwar et al. 2023), and 
IoT (Anwar, Alhalabi, et al. 2024) requires high speed network 
and resources. Thus, Fog computing provides a better solution 
in this domain (Dastjerdi et al. 2016). Zao et al. (2014) proposed 
Fog-­computing-­based infrastructure that perform real-­time 
analysis and signal processing to determine the status of human 
brain in the real world. The aim of the proposed work is to re-
duce the real-­time responsiveness and increase the easiness-­
of-­use. Furthermore, Li et al. (2015) proposed a fog-­computing 
architecture that overcomes the challenges face by XR environ-
ment in cloud-­based solutions. These challenges include the 
computational complexities, network bandwidth, latency sen-
sitivity issues, real-­time data processing and optimisation. The 
proposed architecture enhances the XR experience by efficiently 
processing the input data, rendering output content, and mini-
mising the latency issue for real-­time user interactions.

9.2   |   Security and Privacy
Security and privacy are important concerns that need to be ad-
dressed as a research challenge. Different fog devices want to 
participate in different operations and need to be controlled. A 
certain device that takes part in computation, and hence confi-
dentiality and data loss is certainly an issue. Another security 
issue is user data integrity that possesses and carried out by 
certain device (Khan et al. 2021; Ahmad et al. 2018). To ensure 
the security of a device that has critical information is still a big 
question. Apart from that, a cross-­layer communication between 
devices is still a security concern which needs to be addressed.
9.3   |   Other Fog-­Related Issues
These issues related to fog computing other than security and 
privacy. All of these issues mentioned belonging to fog comput-
ing has immense potential and needs to be addressed as research 
directions shown in Figure 4. Fog computing is a new paradigm 
where it applies the concept of virtualisation as in cloud com-
puting. Various techniques have been suggested so far for better 
utilisation of VM concepts. QoS is an important factor which 
brings in standardisation to computing. Service-­level agreement 
(SLA) and load balancing are the potential factors in fog com-
puting in terms of future research directions.
10   |   Conclusion
In this paper, we present the multi-­faceted fog-­computing RM 
techniques, trends, applications and other aspects. It also pres-
ents the comparison between fog and cloud computing architec-
ture and a discussion on the key aspects in connection to fog 
computing. A taxonomy-­based fog-­computing RM technique 
is discussed along with percentage-­wise research interest. The 
RM techniques include energy awareness, resource allocation, 
scheduling, reliability and scalability. All these features are 
discussed according to the latest research trends in fog comput-
ing. Similarly, fog-­based healthcare 5.0 is a prospect discussed 
with research contributions and limitations and other fog-­based 
application scenarios presented in this particular section. The 
application scenarios along with their characteristics and lim-
itations removed by fog computing are discussed in this par-
ticular section. Fog-­based simulation toolkits were discussed 
subsequently. Finally, we present some challenges that Fog is 
still facing and suggest future research directions. Moreover, 
after discussing the latest trends in fog computing, we mention 
gaps that the computing technology has much potential to ex-
plore things in the future; it will be helpful for modern comput-
ing technology and will bring satisfaction to the users.

Abstract: Due to the recent advancements in high-­speed networks, underlying hardware computing resources and resource scheduling algorithms, Cloud computing has emerged as a popular computing paradigm globally providing end-­user services such as in- frastructure, hardware platforms and application tools. Subsequently, the researchers across various domains have integrated different services to facilitate the end users. However, the real issue faced by the cloud infrastructure is the network latency due to the physical dispersion between clients and cloud data centers. According to an estimate, billions of internet of things (IoT) devices are sharing approximately two exabytes of data daily. Such a huge amount of data can affect network performance if the underlying physical system does not expand up to the required levels, leading to performance degradation. To overcome these issues, a new computing paradigm called Fog Computing has emerged in recent years. In this paper, we discuss the recent developments in fog computing with the integration of real-­time Healthcare 5.0 technology. Furthermore, we describe the pro- posed layered architecture and taxonomy of resource management (RM) techniques in fog computing, which consists of energy awareness, scheduling, reliability and scalability. Besides that, our survey covers the three-­tier layered architecture, evaluation metrics, real-­time application aspects of fog computing and tools providing the implementation of RM techniques in fog com- puting. Furthermore, the proposed layered architecture of the standard fog framework and different state-­of-­the-­art techniques for utilising the computing resources of fog networks have been covered in this study. Moreover, we include various sensors to demonstrate the fog data offloading example in healthcare 5.0 applications. We also present a thorough discussion on various current and future real-­time applications of fog computing. Finally, open challenges and promising future research directions have been identified and discussed in the area of fog-­based real-­time applications. © 2025 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. 2 of 20 Expert Systems, 2025
